title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated licence-plate recognition system, occurring at the point where a machine-generated alert was handed to a human officer in the field. The system matched a plate to a stolen-vehicle record on the basis of a single misread character, and the match was acted on as grounds for a felony stop. The failure sits at the handoff between detection and enforcement, not in the reading itself, since the reader was never designed to be the last word.

Catching it would have required the officer to verify the alert against the plate in front of him before drawing a weapon, which is what the vendor states should happen. The sheriff's office attributed the misread to a tinted plate cover it described as illegal, which places part of the cause in the physical condition of the plate rather than in the software. Both accounts agree the alert alone was not sufficient basis for the detention.

What is not established is whether the plate cover was in fact illegal, whether the misread was caused by it, and whether the deputy's conduct will be reviewed by any outside body. The sheriff's description of the deputy's actions as reasonable is the department's own assessment, not a finding by a court or oversight agency.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, 42, of York County, South Carolina, was detained at gunpoint for over five minutes after a Flock Safety license-plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff's office later said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the malfunction and called the deputy's actions reasonable. Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
